story: In 1971 Qatar was a small, poor pearl-diving peninsula. Then it started exporting the gas from the North Field, the world's largest, which it shares with Iran under the sea, where Iran calls it South Pars. Qatar became, per person, one of the richest countries on Earth, supplier of about a fifth of the world's liquefied natural gas. It built a reputation as everyone's mediator, hosting Hamas's political office and the US military's largest regional base at the same time. In 2026 the war put both its gas and its neutrality under fire.

Iranian drones struck the giant LNG complex at Ras Laffan and the Mesaieed industrial city on 2 March, and QatarEnergy halted production and declared force majeure two days later; with Hormuz effectively closed, it could not ship anyway (Reuters via Pipeline & Gas Journal). On 18 March, after Israel bombed the Iranian side of the shared field, Iranian missiles caused "extensive damage" at Ras Laffan. QatarEnergy's chief said the strike wiped out about 17 percent of export capacity, roughly $20 billion a year in lost revenue, and the company declared force majeure for up to five years on contracts with buyers in Italy, Belgium, South Korea and China (Al Jazeera). European gas prices nearly doubled. Qatar called the attack "blatant aggression" and expelled Iranian officials, a break with years of careful balance with Tehran. Pakistan, not Qatar, became the main US-Iran go-between, though Qatari envoys still shuttled to Tehran.
briefing.power: An absolute hereditary monarchy ruled by the Al Thani family. The emir appoints the prime minister and cabinet; the Shura Council is advisory and, since 2024, fully appointed. Citizens are about 10 percent of the population.
briefing.holders: Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, since 2013; Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani.
